'''''Elodea densa''''', the '''large-flowered waterweed'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''Brazilian waterweed''', is a species of ''[[Elodea]]'' native to warm temperate South America in southeastern [[Brazil]], [[Argentina]], [[Chile]], and [[Uruguay]].<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 2017-12-24}}</ref><ref name=sintesis2014>{{Cite journal|title=El humedal del Río Cruces, Valdivia, Chile: una síntesis ecosistémica|journal=Latin American Journal of Aquatic Research|url=https://scielo.conicyt.cl/scielo.php?pid=S0718-560X2014000500001&script=sci_arttext&tlng=n|last1=Delgado|first1=Luisa E.|volume=42|last2=Tironi|first2=Antonio|issue=5|doi=10.3856/vol42-issue5-fulltext-1|year=2014|language=Spanish|trans-title=The Río Cruces wetland, Valdivia, Chile: an ecosystemic synthesis|last3=Vila|first3=Irma|last4=Verardi|first4=Gabriela|last5=Ibáñez|first5=Carlos|last6=Agüero|first6=Belén|last7=Marín|first7=Víctor H.|pages=937–949 |doi-access=free|hdl=10533/137524|hdl-access=free}}</ref> It is considered a problematic [[Invasive species|invasive]] species due to its use in home aquariums and subsequent release into non-native ecosystems.

== Description ==
[[File:Egeria flower.jpg|thumb|''Elodea densa'' flower]]
''Elodea densa'' is an aquatic plant growing in water up to {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} deep, with trailing stems to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on}} or more long, producing [[root]]s at intervals along the [[Plant stem|stem]]. The leaves are produced in whorls of four to eight, {{convert|1|-|4|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|-|5|mm|in|abbr=on}} broad, with a pointed leaf tip. The stem system of the plant will grow until it reaches the surface of the water, where it will begin to spread out, creating a thick flower [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] that blocks light from reaching plants below it.<ref name=Yarrow>{{cite web |title= The ecology of Egeria densa Planchon (Liliopsida: Alismatales): A wetland ecosystem engineer? |url = http://rchn.biologiachile.cl/pdfs/2009/2/Yarrow_et_al_2009.pdf |publisher=Revista Chilena de Historia Natural 82: 299-313}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=2399368|journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden|volume=75|issue=3|pages=805–810|last1=Haynes|first1=Robert R.|title=Reproductive Biology of Selected Aquatic Plants|year=1988|doi=10.2307/2399368|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/35834 }}</ref> It is [[Plant reproductive morphology|dioecious]], with male and female flowers on separate plants; the flowers are {{convert|12|-|20|mm|in|abbr=on}} diameter, with three broad, rounded, white petals, {{convert|8|-|10|mm|in|abbr=on}} long on male plants, and {{convert|6|-|7|mm|in|abbr=on}} long on female plants.<ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20070621080912/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=4167|title=''Egeria densa''}}</ref><ref name=fna>Flora North America: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220004601 ''Egeria densa'']</ref><ref name=jeps>Jepson Flora: [http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?Egeria+densa ''Egeria densa'']</ref><ref name=wa>Washington Department of Ecology: [http://www.ecy.wa.gov/programs/wq/plants/weeds/aqua002.html ''Egeria densa'']</ref>

=== Life cycle ===
''Elodea densa'' typically displays little variation in growth patterns throughout the year when grown in [[Tropics|tropical]] environments; however, when grown in more moderate environments the plant spends most of its energy on starch production and storage in the winter and canopy growth during the summer season.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Yarrow|first=Mathew|date=2009|title=The ecology of Egeria densa|url=http://rchn.biologiachile.cl/pdfs/2009/2/Yarrow_et_al_2009.pdf|journal=Revista Chilena de Historia Natural}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Elodea densa'' was scientifically described by [[Jules Émile Planchon]] in 1849 and given the name ''Egeria densa'',<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=431710-1 |title=''Elodea densa'' (Planch.) Casp. |access-date=12 October 2024}}</ref> creating the genus ''Egeria''.<ref>{{cite POWO |id=19696-1 |title=''Egeria'' Planch. |access-date=12 October 2024}}</ref> In 1857 [[Robert Caspary]] moved it to genus ''[[Elodea]]''.<ref name="POWO" />

== Habitat and ecology ==
=== Location ===
''Elodea densa'' is native to Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay,<ref name=grin/> and Chile.<ref name=sintesis2014/> As a result of its popularity in [[aquarium]]s the plant has now spread to North America, Europe, Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and Africa.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=20440764|journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment|volume=5|issue=10|pages=528–532|last1=Cohen|first1=Jill|title=Thousands introduced annually: The aquarium pathway for non-indigenous plants to the St Lawrence Seaway|last2=Mirotchnick|first2=Nicholas|last3=Leung|first3=Brian|s2cid=7901599|year=2007|doi=10.1890/060137|bibcode=2007FrEE....5..528C }}</ref>

=== Temperature ===
Temperature is important to the growth of ''Elodea densa;'' however, its growth is mostly stable in temperatures ranging from {{convert|16|-|28|C|F|abbr=on}}, with an upper temperature limit of {{convert|32|C|F|abbr=on}} that results in reduced shoot growth and [[photosynthetic]] output.<ref name=":0" /> Colder temperatures will limit growth of the plant and can be used as a method of controlling its spread in non-native [[ecosystem]]s.{{Citation needed|date=May 2021}}

=== Lighting ===
''Elodea densa'' is able to match photosynthetic output to available light like many [[macrophyte]] species. The species' ability to thrive in low light conditions and its ability to form a dense canopy makes it a very successful invader compared with other macrophytes, resulting in a reduction in the [[Species diversity|diversity]] of plant species where it is introduced.<ref name=":0" />

== Cultivation and uses ==
''Elodea densa'' is a popular aquarium plant, but is no longer sold in some areas due to its [[invasive species|invasive]] potential. Plants in [[Cultivation (agriculture)|cultivation]] are all a male clone, reproducing vegetatively.<ref name=fna/><ref name=jeps/>

It grows well in the cooler aquarium and is suitable for the beginner. It is easily propagated by cuttings. According to reports it secretes [[antibiotic]] substances which can help prevent [[blue-green algae]].<ref>{{citation |url=http://www.tropica.dk/productcard_1.asp?id=058 |title=Egeria densa |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061230130604/http://www.tropica.dk/productcard_1.asp?id=058 |archive-date=2006-12-30 |access-date=2016-09-09 | publisher=Tropica }}</ref> It grows best in a nutrient-rich, high light environment, but has shown an ability to outcompete other species when it is introduced.

=== Economics ===
''E. densa'', like other macrophytes, are effective when used in [[Wastewater treatment|wastewater]] treatment plants due to the same factors that make it a potential invasive plant; mainly its ability to take up nutrients, and sedimentation of particles from the water column.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bishop|first1=Paul L.|last2=Eighmy|first2=T. Taylor|date=1989-01-01|title=Aquatic Wastewater Treatment Using Elodea nuttallii|jstor=25043659|journal=Journal (Water Pollution Control Federation)|volume=61|issue=5|pages=641–648}}</ref>

=== Invasive species ===
''Elodea densa'' has escaped from cultivation and become naturalized and invasive in many warm temperate to subtropical regions of the world, including [[Abkhazia]], [[South Africa]], the [[Azores]], [[Guangdong]], [[Hawaii]], the [[Society Islands]], [[Venezuela]], [[New Zealand]],<ref name=grin/> [[New Caledonia]],<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|title=Les espèces exotiques envahissantes de Nouvelle-Calédonie|last=Hequet|first=Vanessa|year=2009|pages=17|language=fr}}</ref> and North America.<ref name=grin/> In the United States it occurs from [[New York (state)|New York]] south to [[Florida]] and west to [[California]] and [[Oregon]]. In the [[Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta]] of California, it was introduced in the 1960s and has since had a significant adverse impact on the local ecosystem. The plant currently infests {{convert|2400|ha|acre|abbr=on}}, or 12% of the total surface area of the delta, along with other states and even as far north as Canada. Recently, ''E. densa'' was reported as naturalized alien species in [[Iceland]] where it invaded the naturally heated water bodies.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|title = Vallisneria spiralis and Egeria densa (Hydrocharitaceae) in arctic and subarctic Iceland|last1 = Wasowicz|first1 = Pawel|date = 1 August 2014|journal = New Journal of Botany|doi = 10.1179/2042349714Y.0000000043|first2 = Ewa Maria|last2 = Przedpelska-Wasowicz|volume = 4|issue = 2|first3 = Lara|last3 = Gudmundsdottir|last4 = Tamayo|first4 = Mariana|pages = 85–89| bibcode=2014NJBot...4...85W |s2cid = 85764375}}</ref> Due to its occurrence in northern Iceland, ''E. densa'' is one of the first freshwater alien plant species that reached the Arctic.<ref name=":0" /> Most of its impact occurs in the shallow waterways; the plant forms thick mats that obstruct boat passage, clog water intakes and aqueducts, trap sediments, crowd out native vegetation, and impede the migration of [[anadromous]] fish.<ref>Foschi, P. G., Fields, G., & Liu, H. (undated). Detecting a Spectrally Variable Subject in Color Infrared Imagery Using Data-Mining and Knowledge-Engine Methods. ''PRRS04-018''. Available [http://www.public.asu.edu/~huanliu/papers/prrs04.pdf online (pdf file)]</ref><ref name=capc>California Department of Boating and Waterways: [http://www.dbw.ca.gov/aquatic.asp Aquatic Pest Control] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070712101629/http://www.dbw.ca.gov/aquatic.asp |date=2007-07-12 }}</ref>

== Role as ecosystem engineer ==
Though it is sometimes debated, ''E. densa'' is referred to as an [[ecosystem engineer]] as a result of the impact it has on an environment once it is introduced.<ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=3545850|journal=Oikos|volume=69|issue=3|pages=373–386|last1=Jones|first1=Clive G.|title=Organisms as Ecosystem Engineers|last2=Lawton|first2=John H.|last3=Shachak|first3=Moshe|year=1994|doi=10.2307/3545850|bibcode=1994Oikos..69..373J }}</ref> Some of these impacts are due to its fast growth and high [[Biological dispersal|dispersal]] rate when fragmented, its ability to adapt to different light and nutrient availability, its uptake of nutrients from the water column and its effect on sedimentation of these nutrients, and the large light-blocking canopy that its flowers form at the surface of the water.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=23213755|journal=Ecology|volume=93|issue=6|pages=1262–1268|last1=Wright|first1=Jeffrey T.|title=Invasive ecosystem engineer selects for different phenotypes of an associated native species|last2=Gribben|first2=Paul E.|last3=Byers|first3=James E.|last4=Monro|first4=Keyne|year=2012|doi=10.1890/11-1740.1|pmid=22834366|url=https://espace.library.uq.edu.au/view/UQ:277120/UQ277120_OA.pdf|doi-access=free|bibcode=2012Ecol...93.1262W }}</ref>

''Elodea densa'' is also responsible for changing the amount of [[phytoplankton]] present in the water column due to limiting light availability from the dense [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] that it forms, and from the amount of nutrients that removes from the water column. It can, however, also function as shelter for [[zooplankton]] and smaller invertebrates.<ref name=":0" />

[[Black-necked swan]]s feed on the plant, and decline of ''E. densa'' has been linked to the decline of swan populations.<ref name=sintesis2014/>

== Control ==
A variety of methods are needed to ensure that growth of ''E. densa'' is stopped due to its ability to regrow when fragmented through mechanical means. The best way is to remove the plant in entirety from the [[water column]] or use herbicides to kill the plant.<ref>{{Cite journal|jstor=2443637|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=71|issue=1|pages=162–163|last1=Steward|first1=Kerry K.|title=Hydrilla Invades Washington, D.C. And the Potomac|last2=Van|first2=Thai K.|last3=Carter|first3=Virginia|last4=Pieterse|first4=Arnold H.|year=1984|doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1984.tb12498.x}}</ref> One of the potential solutions to the problem are water [[Drawdown (hydrology)|drawdowns]], as the plant is very sensitive to drying out and the plant can die in as short as an hour when removed from water. In addition cold weather has been found to be effective in controlling the plant, though this has practical limitations.<ref name=":0" /> When [[herbicide]]s were applied to the plant, the levels of phosphorus and nitrogen increased but not greatly, suggesting that most of the nutrients remained in the plant biomass and did not reabsorb into the water column.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Strange|first=Richard J.|date=1976-01-01|title=Nutrient Release and Community Metabolism Following Application of Herbicide to Macrophytes in Microcosms|jstor=2402264|journal=Journal of Applied Ecology|volume=13|issue=3|pages=889–897|doi=10.2307/2402264|bibcode=1976JApEc..13..889S }}</ref>
